title: Big Walk, the Year's Best-Reviewed Game, Reveals How Ordinary Loneliness Really Looks
excerpt: House House's co-op-only puzzle game has sold over a million copies in six days — and sparked a broader conversation about what happens when a game requires friends you may not have.
body:
• Big Walk, the new co-op game from Untitled Goose Game developer House House, has become the highest-rated game of 2026 on Metacritic with a score of 93 and sold over one million copies in six days.
  • The game requires two to 12 players with no solo mode or public matchmaking, forcing players who lack a ready friend group to seek companions on Reddit and forums.
  • Critics praise its design for exploring both connection and loneliness — players get lost, separated, and must find their way back to friends using limited communication tools.
  • The game's friend requirement has ignited debate about accessibility and social isolation in an era when loneliness is a recognized public health crisis.

The most acclaimed video game of 2026 is, at its core, about a very simple thing: going for a walk with your friends. But Big Walk, the co-op puzzle adventure from Australian studio House House, has also become an unlikely mirror for something far less comfortable — the quiet, pervasive loneliness that shapes millions of lives.

Released on August 4 for PC, PlayStation 5, and Nintendo Switch 2, the game sold over one million copies in just six days, according to publisher Panic Games. It currently holds a 93 on Metacritic, making it the best-reviewed new release of the year, ahead of titles like Forza Horizon 6 and Mina the Hollower.

A Game That Demands Company

What makes Big Walk distinctive — and controversial — is what it refuses to offer. There is no solo mode. There is no online matchmaking. There are no public lobbies. To play, you need between two and 12 friends who own copies of the game, devices to run it on, and the willingness to coordinate schedules across multiple sessions. The game takes roughly 15 hours to complete.

For players without a ready group, Big Walk's subreddit became a meeting ground within hours of launch. A megathread accumulated over 200 requests from people looking for companions, saturated with time-zone-specific posts and simple pleas: "Wanna play?"

"Basically, you have to have friends to play Big Walk."

— Kotaku

House House, the Melbourne-based studio behind 2019's Untitled Goose Game, designed these constraints deliberately. The game was born during the COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns, when the studio channeled fears of permanent social isolation into a game about getting lost in nature with friends, according to Polygon.

Connection and Its Absence

In Big Walk, players control small, bloblike characters exploring an uninhabited island filled with puzzles that require teamwork to solve. Communication happens through proximity voice chat — voices fade with distance, echo through corridors, muffle through walls. Players can gesture, ring cowbells, fire flare guns, or use walkie-talkies, but can only hold one item at a time.

Inevitably, players get separated. Someone wanders off into the trees. Night falls and visibility drops. Friends disappear. The experience of being alone in the dark, calling into your microphone and hearing nothing back, is by design.

"Big Walk is as much a game about loneliness as it is about connection," wrote Kotaku's Rebekah Valentine in her review. "There's also a profundity in quiet moments in the dark, alone, unsure if your friends have a walkie-talkie with which to hear you calling."

The Loneliness Debate

The game's strict friend requirement has illuminated a tension that extends well beyond gaming. In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General declared loneliness and social isolation a public health epidemic, noting links to a 29% increased risk of heart disease, a 50% increased risk of dementia, and a more than 60% increased risk of premature death.

For the players flooding Reddit with requests to find strangers to walk with, Big Walk presents a peculiar paradox: a game about friendship that reveals how many people struggle to assemble even a small group willing to spend time together.

GameRant noted that while the game's reviews are "borderline perfect," its requirement for a "cohesive and constant group that won't get bored, refund, or be too busy" represents a fundamental barrier. The game "looks like a charming and genuinely unique co-op game that virtually everyone can get involved in," the outlet wrote, but its brilliance "remains gated behind" having the right social infrastructure.

By Design, Not by Accident

Not everyone sees this as a flaw. Kotaku's Zack Zwiezen argued that adding a solo mode "would completely ruin Big Walk" and that "it's okay for games to not compromise their design or vision to make them accessible to everyone in all situations."

The game's commercial success suggests the design gamble is paying off. But the conversation it has sparked — about who gets to participate in shared experiences, and who is left on the outside looking in — resonates far beyond the screen.

As Valentine wrote in her review: "Everyone is busy, life is hard, and the world is falling apart. There is no better time to call up your friends."
